title: Is There No Balm in Gilead?
summary: The bones of Judah's leaders will be dug up and spread before the sun and stars they worshiped. God asks why his people turn away and never turn back, when even migrating birds know their seasons; the wise have rejected his word, and the prophets still cry peace. As the enemy's horses snort from Dan, the people despair, and the prophet breaks into grief, crying that the harvest is past and no one is saved, and asking whether there is no balm in Gilead.
story: Chapter 8 continues the section that began with the temple sermon in chapter 7. Its first three verses finish the prose judgment on Topheth, and then the chapter returns to poetry. It gathers themes already sounded (the refusal to return, false prophets who cry peace, the enemy from the north) and moves toward something new: the grief of the one who announces the judgment. The final verses of this chapter and the first verse of chapter 9 are among the most personal laments in the Bible, and they have earned Jeremiah his traditional name, the weeping prophet.
historical:
The chapter's setting is the same period as chapter 7, the reign of Jehoiakim (609 to 598 BC), with the Babylonian threat growing after Nebuchadnezzar's victory at Carchemish in 605 BC. The astral worship of verse 2, sun, moon, and the host of heaven, had been promoted by King Manasseh (2 Kings 21:3-5), who reigned for much of the seventh century, and though Josiah removed it (2 Kings 23:4-5, 11) it evidently survived. Digging up the bones of the dead was a known act of desecration in the ancient Near East; Josiah himself had burned the bones from the tombs at Bethel on the altar there (2 Kings 23:16).

Gilead, the hilly region east of the Jordan, was known for its balm, an aromatic resin used as medicine and traded widely; the Ishmaelite traders who bought Joseph were carrying balm from Gilead to Egypt (Genesis 37:25). Dan (verse 16) was the northernmost town of the land, so the snorting of horses heard from Dan meant the invaders had entered the country.
cultural:
Burial mattered deeply in ancient Israel. To be buried with one's ancestors was a final dignity, and to lie unburied, scattered like dung, was the ultimate curse (Deuteronomy 28:26). The irony of verse 2 is sharp: the leaders will be spread out before the very sun, moon, and stars they served, and those gods will do nothing for them.

The land of Israel lies on one of the world's great bird migration routes, along the Jordan Valley between Africa and Europe and Asia, and every spring and autumn huge flocks of storks and other birds pass over. Jeremiah's hearers would have watched them come and go on schedule. The birds follow the order God built into creation; God's people do not follow his requirements. Verse 20 draws on the farming year: the grain harvest came in spring and early summer, and the summer fruit (figs, grapes) in late summer. If both failed, there would be no food for winter. The phrase meant that every chance has passed. Snake charmers (verse 17) were a familiar sight in the ancient world; a snake that could not be charmed was beyond all remedy.
literary: The chapter mixes prose (verses 1 to 3) with poetry and moves between several voices, which can be hard to separate. God speaks in verses 4 to 13 and 17; the people speak in verses 14 and 15 and in the quoted cries of verses 19 and 20; and the prophet speaks in verses 18 to 22. At points God and prophet seem to share one voice of grief, so that interpreters differ over who is weeping. Verses 10 to 12 repeat 6:12-15 almost word for word. The Hebrew verb shuv (to turn or return) is played on repeatedly in verses 4 and 5: do people turn away and not turn back? In the Hebrew Bible, chapter 8 continues one more verse, so the English 9:1 (Oh, that my head were a spring of water) is Hebrew 8:23, closing this lament.

outline.t: The bones spread before the sun and stars
Why do they never return? The stork knows its time
False wisdom and a lying pen
No harvest, and horses from Dan
The prophet's grief: no balm in Gilead

doctrines.note: People who fall get up, and people who wander come back, yet Judah refuses to return. No one asks, What have I done? Repentance begins with that honest question, and its absence is what makes the people's case so hopeless.

The people claim to be wise and to have the Law of the LORD, but they have rejected his word. Having Scripture is not the same as heeding it, and interpreters who bend it to suit themselves turn it into a deception.
The prophet's sorrow is beyond healing. He shares the pain of the people he must condemn, showing that judgment spoken by God's servants should come with tears, not with satisfaction.

words.note: Torah, law or instruction. It means more than a legal code: it is God's teaching for how his people should live. In verse 8 the people boast that the Law of the LORD is with them, yet the lying pen of the scribes has made it a deception. Scholars differ on whether this means scribes who falsified written law, or interpreters who used genuine law to justify disobedience; either way, possessing the Torah had become a substitute for obeying it.

Mishpat, justice or ordinance, here the requirements of the LORD. Verse 7 contrasts birds that know their appointed times with a people that does not know God's mishpat. The word covers both the order God sets and the just decisions that follow from it.

Tsori, balm, a resin from Gilead used to soothe and heal wounds. Jeremiah asks whether there is no balm in Gilead and no physician there. The healing was available, but the people refused it. The question later became a line in an African American spiritual that answers it: there is a balm in Gilead.

Shever, breaking, fracture, or ruin. The false prophets heal the people's shever lightly (verse 11), and the prophet is crushed by the shever of his people (verse 21). The word links the prophets' failure with the prophet's grief: they ignored the fracture; he feels it.

christ: Jeremiah weeping over a people who would not be healed prepares for Jesus weeping over Jerusalem because it did not recognize the time of its visitation (Luke 19:41-44). Some in Jesus's day thought he was Jeremiah come back (Matthew 16:14), perhaps because of this pattern of grief and rejection. The question of verse 22, whether there is a physician for God's wounded people, is answered in the Gospels by Jesus, who said he came as a physician for the sick (Mark 2:17), and 1 Peter 2:24 says that by his wounds we are healed. These are thematic links, not predictions in Jeremiah, but they show where the prophet's longing for healing finds its answer. The lament that the harvest is past and we are not saved also sharpens the New Testament's urgency about the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2).

hard.q: Who is weeping in verses 18 to 22: Jeremiah, or God?
hard.a:
The speaker in verses 18 to 22 says my sorrow, my heart, the daughter of my people. Most readers assume it is Jeremiah, and the chapter supports that: he is the one who hears the people's cry from a far land. Yet the lines are interrupted in verse 19 by God's own question, Why have they provoked Me to anger, and the phrase daughter of My people is used by God elsewhere in the same chapter (verse 11). Some interpreters therefore hear God himself grieving through the prophet's voice, or the prophet's grief so fully sharing God's that the two cannot be separated.

The ambiguity may be deliberate. The book presents Jeremiah as one whose life mirrors God's word, and whose tears reflect God's own pain over his people. Readers who hold that God cannot suffer in the way humans do (the classical doctrine of divine impassibility) and readers who stress God's real emotional involvement can agree that the passage shows judgment is not delivered in cold anger. Whether the tears are the prophet's, God's, or both, the chapter insists that the one who judges is not indifferent.

questions: The stork knows its seasons, but God's people do not know his requirements. What in your own life shows that you know God's ways, or that you do not?
Having the Law did not make the people wise. How can knowing a lot about the Bible become a substitute for obeying it?
Is there no balm in Gilead? Where do you need healing that you have been refusing, and what might it take to accept it?
